rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to ensure all 10 compounds elute within the 42 min window while giving enough spread to estimate the true elution window and identify critical pairs. This run is a balanced first map of retention versus composition without risking an overly truncated method.

All compounds eluted early and well within the gradient, so trim the solvent window to the actual elution region to spend gradient time where the peaks are and improve efficiency without risking loss of compounds. Keeping tG and T fixed isolates the effect of narrowing the phi window on the closest cluster around peaks 5–7.

The broad window was better than the trimmed one, so now test slope sensitivity by halving tG while keeping phi and T fixed. Comparing this directly to injection 1 will show whether the critical mid-cluster is helped by shallower or steeper gradients and may improve CRF via shorter run time if resolution stays adequate.

The 10 min gradient was fast but over-compressed the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min gave full resolution, so a longer run will map how strongly that pair responds to slope and help bracket the optimum tG. This direct slope study at the same phi window and temperature is the fastest way to tune the tradeoff between CRF time penalty and the unresolved mid-cluster.

The optimum should lie between 10 and 20 min: 10 min is fastest but under-resolves the 5–7 cluster, while 20 min is fully resolved but slower. A 14 min gradient directly probes that middle ground and is likely to improve the current best CRF if it lifts the worst-pair resolution enough with only a modest time penalty.

The best point so far is near the slope threshold where pair 6–7 just becomes adequately resolved, so make a small increase from 14 to 16 min at the same phi window and temperature. This should improve that critical pair with only a slight time cost and may reach the CRF maximum if full resolution is restored before any time penalty appears.

At 14 min the only deficiency is the 6–7 pair, and slope changes have already bracketed the optimum, so temperature is now the best lever to alter selectivity without much run-time cost. A modest drop to 35 C may separate that close pair enough to retain the zero time penalty and beat the current best CRF.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by shifting the critical coelution earlier in the cluster, so test the opposite direction at the best 14 min gradient. A small increase to 45 C is the cleanest way to see whether temperature can improve the 6–7 pair while preserving the favorable zero time penalty.

Since only even tG values are allowed, probe the other side of the 14 min optimum to better bracket the slope-response threshold of the critical cluster. A 12 min run may still keep zero time penalty while showing how sharply CRF drops as the 6–7 pair compresses.

The broad 0.05–0.95 window may be slightly steeper than needed because the last peak still elutes very early, so trim only the high-organic end while keeping the successful 14 min slope region and 40 C. This mild narrowing could improve spacing in the 5–7 cluster without pushing the run into a time-penalty regime or disturbing early peaks much.

Trimming phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6–7 pair while keeping zero time penalty, so continue in the same direction with a slightly narrower high-end window. This should further shallow the effective gradient and may push the worst-pair resolution to the optimum without making the run long enough to incur a time penalty.

The 0.05–0.90 window improved selectivity versus 0.95, but 0.85 incurred a small time penalty, so the sweet spot may be slightly steeper. Testing the same narrowed window at 12 min checks whether we can keep the selectivity gain from phi1 = 0.90 while shortening the run enough to improve on the current best CRF.

The optimum is clearly near phi1 = 0.90 and tG = 14 min, so now test whether slightly raising phi0 helps by trimming excess low-organic time while keeping the same upper window. This can subtly reshape the effective gradient over the crowded middle region and may improve the 6–7 pair without increasing overall run time.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF further while keeping zero time penalty, suggesting the low-end window was still broader than necessary. A small additional increase to phi0 = 0.15 at the same phi1, tG, and T may further optimize selectivity in the crowded middle cluster while still retaining all peaks comfortably.

The best method is now centered at phi0 = 0.10, phi1 = 0.90, and narrowing phi1 previously increased the critical-pair resolution at the cost of only a small time shift. Combining the best phi0 with the narrower upper limit may improve the 6–7 pair enough to outweigh any slight time penalty and could surpass the current best CRF.

We have already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000, so further runs should protect against missing an equally optimal neighboring plateau while avoiding repeats. Testing a slightly narrower upper window checks whether the optimum is robust or if 0.85 is the sharp upper bound before time penalty or over-retention appears.

Now that 0.10–0.85 at 14 min and 40 C is confirmed optimal, explore whether a slightly higher phi0 can maintain full resolution while shortening the late end or improving robustness around the first peaks. This is a close neighbor of the optimum and one of the few remaining plausible plateau points for CRF = 1.000.

Two adjacent methods at phi1 = 0.85 have reached CRF 1.000, so map the plateau boundary by increasing phi0 one more step. This checks whether the optimum region extends upward in phi0 or whether early peaks begin to approach the unretained limit and degrade robustness.

With CRF already at the maximum, the remaining useful information is the local plateau shape around the optimum. Testing a slightly shallower gradient at one optimal phi window checks robustness and whether full resolution is maintained with only a negligible time cost, confirming how broad the true optimum region is.

The optimum clearly depends on zero time penalty more than extra resolution, so test the steeper side of the other CRF 1.000 window. This will show whether the 0.15–0.85 composition remains on the optimal plateau at shorter tG or falls off faster than the 0.10–0.85 case.

With the maximum already reached, use remaining runs to compare robustness of the optimum plateau to temperature at the best composition window. This checks whether the perfect method is sharply temperature-specific or whether a warmer setting preserves the plateau, which is valuable if multiple methods tie in score.

We have shown the optimum collapses at higher temperature for one perfect composition, so test the other CRF 1.000 composition at lower temperature to complete the robustness picture. This also checks whether the two optimal windows behave symmetrically with temperature or if one is intrinsically more stable.

With only a few injections left and the optimum already found, map one remaining nearby corner of composition–slope space that could in principle still score perfectly by trading some of the extra resolution from phi1 = 0.80 for a shorter gradient. This helps close the local response surface around the optimum without repeating known losers.

One untested near-optimal neighbor is the higher-phi0 version of the strong 0.15–0.90 method. This probes the upper edge of the apparent phi0 plateau while keeping the broader upper window that previously avoided time penalty, and it may reveal another CRF 1.000 condition.

For the final shot, test the remaining nearby corner that could still plausibly reach the full-resolution/acceptable-time boundary: a slightly shallower version of the fully resolved 0.05–0.85 window. This closes the last meaningful gap in the local design space around the confirmed optimum plateau without repeating any prior method.
